blocks.p: Dear Stephen, found a grey hair in my eyebrow this morning and laughed out loud in the washroom like a fool. Four hundred years in this face, and it has finally decided to keep a record. I find I don’t mind. It’s the first thing in a long while that has been honest with me.
Lyda Thorne had watched thousands of people lie down in the cold, and she had never once lain down herself.

She told Sol so on the evening he came back to Philippa, fourteen months after he had first woken there. She was standing at the foot of the Linnet’s ramp with a ledger under her arm, as she stood at the foot of every Thorne ramp that came in while she was in the yard, and she watched him come down it, one hand on the rail, and looked at him the way she looked at a hull back from a long run: carefully, all over, for damage.
“You’ve stopped,” she said.
“Stopped?”

“Getting old at me.” She tucked the ledger closer. “Every time you came down one of these, you’d have another year on you. I used to stand here and count. Lucan wrote from Berea and said it had slowed. I didn’t believe him till now.”

It was true. Lucan had measured him in the Linnet’s cramped surgery on the way home, with calipers and a light and a long list of questions, and pronounced the account settled: about fifty-two in the body, the doctor thought, and from here on he would age a year a year, like anyone. Sol had looked into the small steel mirror over the basin while Lucan wrote it down. Grey all through, the lines at his mouth and between his brows set now, the skin of his neck a little loose. A face that would go on changing for the rest of his life, slowly, the way faces had changed in the world before. He had found that he did not mind it.
“Welcome to the rest of us, Bishop,” Lyda said.

Her letter had found him on Berea, two months before. He had written to her from Galatia about the laboratory and the rain and the fuse, three close pages of it, and she had answered him in one line in her square, impatient hand: Tell the Pasks to wait. Lucan’s already started. L. He had read it standing on the dock at Berea and laughed aloud, and the Berean deacon beside him had asked whether it was good news, and he had not known how to answer.

They walked up through the yard together in the long Philippa dusk. The cranes stood against the sky like herons, and the loaders were going home, and somewhere a crew was singing, badly, a song Sol did not know. Lyda talked about cargo. She talked about a hull on the slip with a cracked keel and a shipmaster on Ephes who had stopped paying, and he listened, and did not mind that either. He had spent his whole remembered life among people who talked only about what they wanted. She talked about what was broken and what it would cost to fix.

“I’ve got every manifest you’ve been on,” she said, without looking at him. “Since the Kestrel. I know where you’ve been to the hour.” She walked a few steps. “That’s not a confession. It’s my line. I know where everything on it is.”
“I know,” he said.

“I’ve never been off this world,” Lyda said. “Not once. Thirty-six years. I’ve put more people in those pods than live on this river, Sol, and closed the lids on them, and watched the frost come up, and gone home. And every time you go, I go home.” She stopped by the gate of the yard office and stood with her hand on it. “I don’t like it. I didn’t used to mind. Now I don’t like it.”

She had called him by his name. It went through him the way the first word in the market had gone through him, a long time ago, and he stood very still so as not to let it show, and knew that it showed.

Lucan had been building it since Galatia, at a folding bench in the Linnet’s surgery between crossings, and he finished it in three days in the cellar under the infirmary, beside the relay that hummed with heaven’s noise. He laid it out for them on a clean cloth under the lamp: a sliver no larger than a fingernail paring, a dark square and, around it, fine as a hair, a ring of wire.
Sol looked at it for a long moment before he could speak.

“It’s everything a Halo has,” Lucan said, in his lecturing voice, which was how he said things when he was proud of them. “The pulse that keeps the body alive in the cold. The governor that wakes it at the other end. The recorder too, I’m afraid; it’s so tangled into the rest that I couldn’t take it out without breaking the pulse, so I left it, and gave it nowhere to send. What it hasn’t got is an uplink. No tuning to Sion. There’s no line out of it at all. It will keep you alive through a crossing, and it will talk to no one.” He looked at Lyda. “A local neural. Your own private Halo, if you want to be grand about it.”
“I don’t,” Lyda said.
“Where’s the write path?” Sol said.
Lucan glanced at him. “There’s no uplink, Tarren. Nothing outside could reach it.”
“Where is it?”
Lucan considered him, and then turned the lamp and set the sliver under the microscope at the end of the bench, and stepped back.

Sol bent to the eyepiece. It was there, at one edge of the chip, where two pathways met: a bridge of metal finer than a hair. It looked exactly as it had looked through another microscope in another life, with rain on the window. He picked up the fine probe from the bench. His hand was not smooth anymore. The knuckles were thick and the tremor was there when he held it still, and he did what he had done then: he set his wrist on the bench and let the bench be steady for him. He set the tip of the probe against the bridge.
“So your hand’s touching my head after all,” Lyda said behind him, quietly.
“Only to shut the door.”
He pressed the key. There was a small bright spark under the glass, and a thread of smoke too small to smell, and the bridge was gone.
He straightened. His back told him about it. Lyda was looking at him, not at the microscope, with an expression he had not seen on her before and could not read.
“Again, if you’d like,” Lucan said dryly. “It won’t get any more burned.”
“Once is enough,” Sol said. “Once was always supposed to be enough.”

She would not have it at the temple. “I’ve gone thirty-six years without a coin in my face,” she said, “and I’m not going to start looking pious now.” So Lucan put it behind her left ear, where the bone was close and the hair would cover it, and where, he said, the pulse would reach as well as anywhere.

She lay on the cot in the infirmary’s back room with her head turned on the pillow, and Lucan numbed the place and shaved a small square and cleaned it, and laid out his instruments on the cloth: fine and bright and very small. Sol sat on the other side of the cot. He had not been asked to. When Lucan picked up the first instrument, Lyda put out her hand across the blanket without looking, and Sol took it, and she held on.
“Talk to me,” she said. “Not about this.”
“What about?”
“Anything. Tobin says God knows everything in my head already.”
“Yes.”
“Without a coin.”
“He doesn’t need one.”
“That’s worse,” Lyda said.
Lucan, bent close over her ear, made a small sound that might have been a laugh.

“Does he take anything?” she said. “When he reads you. I’ve watched your machine at work all my life. People go into renewal on this world carrying something and come out without it, and they can’t tell you what it was. And they’re glad.” Her hand had tightened. “Does yours do that?”
“No,” Sol said. “He doesn’t take anything.”
“Then what does he want with it all?”
Sol thought of the psalm in the granary, and a boy stumbling through it at the end of the day. Search me, and know my heart. “You,” he said.

She did not answer. She lay with her eyes on the wall and her hand in his, and Lucan worked in silence, and the little instruments made their small precise sounds against the cloth. After a while Sol felt her thumb move once across the back of his hand, over the brown spot there, and stop.
“Done,” Lucan said. “Don’t touch it. Don’t wash your hair for three days. Don’t cross for a week.”
“I wasn’t planning to wash my hair,” said Lyda, “and I’ve waited my whole life to cross. I can wait a week.”

But afterward, when Lucan had gone and the lamp was low, she lay on the cot with her eyes closed, and said, so quietly that he almost did not hear: “I don’t believe it, you know. Any of it. I’d like to.” A pause. “That’s new. The liking to.”
The Linnet sailed eight days later for Daphne.

Teo was on the crew list as pilot trainee, and he went down the passenger hold ahead of them checking the pods with a seriousness Sol had never seen on him, running his hand along each seal. When he came to the two at the end of the row, side by side, he checked his sister’s twice.
“I’ve closed a thousand of these,” he told her.
“You’ve closed eleven,” said Lyda. “I’ve got the logs.”

The hold was cold and blue-lit and smelled of coolant, and the pods stood in their two long rows like upright coffins, as they had stood in the Kestrel’s hold on Plenty a lifetime ago. Down the rows the lids had already gone white, one after another, over faces he could no longer see. Lucan was at the end of the row with a small instrument of his own making that would read the pulse in Lyda’s implant through the glass. He had not said he was worried. He had checked the instrument four times.
Lyda stood looking down into her pod. Sol had seen her face do many things in fourteen months. He had not seen it afraid.
She’ll wake as nothing.

It came quietly, in his own voice, flattened, with the faint crackle under it like a signal through bad weather. She’ll wake as nothing, or she won’t wake. You put it in her. Your hand. Your hand on the burn. She’ll die in the cold and it will be your hand, the way it was always your hand, your hand, your...
“Christ,” Sol said under his breath, and the voice shattered into hiss and stopped.
Lyda had heard him. She turned her head. “Is it the noise?”
“Yes.”
“What does it say?”
“That I’ll kill you.”
She looked at him steadily. “Will you?”
“No.”
“Then say it again,” Lyda said. “Not under your breath. Out loud. I want to hear it.”

He had said it aloud in a hundred house churches, to people who had come to hear it. He had never said it to her. He said it, plainly, in the cold blue air, and it did not echo, and nothing happened, except that Lyda Thorne, who had spent her life staying just far enough inside the church to be left alone, stood and heard a forbidden word spoken in her own ship and did not flinch.
“I can’t do it,” she said. “Whatever it is that Tobin does. Whatever you do. I don’t know how.” She looked down into the pod. “You do it. For both of us. Just this once.”

So he prayed. He did not have many words for it yet, and he used the ones he had been given. “If I go up to the heavens, you are there,” he said. “If I make my bed in the depths, you are there. Even the darkness is not dark to you.” He stopped. “Keep her. Wake her. Amen.”
“Amen,” said Teo, from the end of the row, and went red.

Lyda climbed in. She lay back on the padding with her hands at her sides and her jaw set, the way he had seen her stand at the foot of a ramp in a high wind. Sol climbed into the pod beside hers, slowly, and his knees told him about it, and he lay back. The padding gave under him, stiff with cold. Between the two pods there was an arm’s length of air, and she reached across it, and he took her hand.
“Lyda,” he said.
“What.”
“I love you.”
She did not turn her head. She lay looking up at the ribbed ceiling of the hold, and he saw her throat move.
“I know,” she said. “Tell me on the other side. I want to be sure I’m awake for it.”
Teo came down the row and closed her lid. Then he came to Sol’s, and stood a moment with his hand on it, looking down at him with his young face very serious, and closed that too.

The cold came in from the edges. White crept over the glass above his face, and through it he could see nothing of her, only the blue light thickening and going away. Somewhere under his ribs his heart had begun to take its time. He thought of her heart slowing in the next pod, kept by a sliver of silicon no bigger than a fingernail paring, a pulse in the cold, Stephen’s half, with nothing in it of his but a door burned shut.
Then he went down into it, and did not feel himself go.

He woke to warmth and a hiss of air and the ache of his whole body coming back to itself. The frost on the glass above him was running in long clear threads. Someone had opened his lid. He turned his head on the padding.
Her pod was still frosted white.

Lucan was kneeling beside it with his instrument against the glass. He did not look up. Teo stood behind him with both hands clenched at his sides. Sol lay and watched the frost on her pod and did not breathe, and the hold was very quiet, and somewhere along the row other sleepers were waking with soft hisses, one after another, and hers did not.
“Pulse is there,” Lucan said, very low. “It’s there. It’s slow. It’s coming up.”
The frost on her glass began to run.

It went in threads, the way his own had gone, clear lines spreading down through the white, and behind them he could see the shape of her face, pale, eyes shut, and then the lid hissed and lifted, and warm air poured in, and Lyda Thorne drew one long hard breath like someone surfacing from deep water, and opened her eyes.
She looked at the ceiling. Then she turned her head and found him.
“Well?” she said. Her voice was hoarse and furious and very much alive. “I’m awake.”
Sol had gotten himself out of his pod, badly, and was kneeling on the deck beside hers. “I love you,” he said.
“I heard you the first time.” She lay looking at him. Her hand came out over the edge of the pod and found his face, and stayed there. “I came, didn’t I,” she said. “I came.”
“You came.”
“I love you, Sol,” Lyda said, as plainly as she said everything, as if it were a figure in a ledger that she had checked many times and found correct. “Now help me out of this thing.”

He helped her out. She stood on the deck holding his arm, unsteady, while Lucan shone his light in her eyes and asked her questions and wrote down the answers, and Teo turned away and wiped his face with his sleeve and pretended he had not.
Then the outer hatch opened, and the ramp ran down, and the air of another world came in.

It smelled green. That was the first thing: green and wet and alive, after the coolant and cold of the hold, the smell of a great many growing things very close together. The light was soft and a little gold. Beyond the end of the ramp the port gave way to low hills furred with something that moved in the wind like grass and was not quite grass, and over them stood a sky Lyda Thorne had never seen.
She walked down the ramp slowly, holding his arm. At the bottom she stopped and stood with her face lifted, and did not say anything for a long time.

Sol watched her. He had seen a hundred worlds and stood under a hundred skies, and he could not remember a single one of them the way he would remember this: her face turned up to a sky that was new to her, and the tears running down it openly, and her not wiping them away.

She was going to die. He had known it since the night he first understood what she was: a woman with no coin and no backup and no City, who would grow old in front of him and go down into the ground the way the whole world had gone before the mercy. He had lived four hundred years among people who could not die, and he had never once loved any of them like this.
She would die. So would he. They would grow old, and they would do it side by side, a year a year, like anyone.
He stood at the foot of the ramp holding her arm, and found that he could bear it.
